strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical impact on MLLM inference efficiency
Comprehensive evaluation across 13 diverse benchmarks (7 image, 6 video) with multiple model sizes
Strong empirical results achieving 3-4× token reduction (80% to 23-25% ratio) with minimal or improved accuracy
Practical post-training approach applicable to already-trained models without retraining from scratch
Inference-aligned optimization using variable token budgets to explore efficiency-performance tradeoff
Sensible use of KL divergence regularization to minimize transfer entropy from sparse attention
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing GRPO algorithm to existing ZipVL mechanism without algorithmic innovations
Missing critical ablation studies: no analysis of reward weighting, KL weight β sensitivity, or hyperparameter impact
Insufficient comparisons: methods mentioned in introduction (MOBA, NSA, MInference) are not empirically compared; no comparison with simpler baselines
Lack of analytical depth: no investigation of what the model learns differently, attention pattern analysis, or mechanistic understanding of improvements
Reproducibility concerns: missing hyperparameters (learning rate, optimizer, iterations, batch size), evaluation setting differences, and no code availability mentioned
Questionable design justification: equal weighting of performance and efficiency rewards presented without ablation or theoretical justification
No ablation studies on reward formulation: binary accuracy and (1-τ) efficiency are presented without exploring alternative designs or their necessity
Limited error analysis: no per-benchmark analysis, no statistical significance testing, no identification of failure modes or edge cases
Presentation issues: paper is very brief with insufficient technical depth; Figure 1 is cluttered; key concepts like 'sampling group' inadequately explained
Overclaimed contributions: characterizes application of existing GRPO and ZipVL as 'novel' methods; lacks original algorithmic or architectural contributions

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem of token sparsity in MLLMs with direct relevance to computational efficiency
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 13 benchmarks (7 image + 6 video) and three model sizes demonstrates broad applicability
Achieves impressive quantitative results with ~75% token reduction (80%→25%) while maintaining competitive accuracy
Post-training approach is pragmatic and can be applied to already well-trained models without retraining from scratch
Optimization pipeline is well-aligned with actual inference process, treating sparse attention as policy model
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: simply applies existing GRPO algorithm to existing ZipVL sparse attention with trivial reward function (binary accuracy + token reduction); no novel algorithmic insights or theoretical contributions

Critical ablation studies missing: no ablations on reward function design, KL weight β sensitivity, or contribution of individual components; unclear whether improvements come from GRPO, reward design, or largely from ZipVL itself

Insufficient methodological clarity: performance reward computation unspecified; relationship between p∼U(0,1) and token reduction unclear; token ratio τ computation vague; missing crucial hyperparameters (N, ε, β values); calibration data splits undisclosed

Incomplete experimental analysis lacking layer-wise pruning analysis, statistical significance testing, and clear attribution of improvements; results sometimes ambiguous (e.g., accuracy differences <0.5% without confidence intervals)
No baseline comparisons with alternative efficiency methods, knowledge distillation, or other RL approaches; single calibration dataset (Video-R1-260k) with unknown generalization properties

Weak justification for design choices: why equal weighting (1:1) of performance and efficiency rewards? Why binary accuracy instead of continuous? Why GRPO over other RL algorithms? No Pareto frontier analysis

Limited scope despite broad benchmarks: evaluation only on Qwen models; generalization to other architectures (LLaVA, etc.) unknown; stated differences from official benchmark results raise reproducibility concerns
Reproducibility issues: no code/model release mentioned, many hyperparameters missing, evaluation protocol differs from official benchmarks, integration of ZipVL with GRPO policy optimization unclear
Incomplete presentation: only 4 pages suggesting rushed work; Figure 1 lacks clarity; related work section missing; 'minimal' accuracy reduction claims need quantification and significance testing
Trivial reward function design without justification or alternatives explored; cannot distinguish contribution of GRPO from straightforward application of existing components

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical token efficiency challenges in MLLMs
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 13 benchmarks spanning image and video understanding tasks
Pragmatic post-training approach applicable to already well-trained models without retraining from scratch
Achieves significant token reduction (80% to 22-25%) with relatively stable accuracy across multiple model variants
Generally clear presentation with well-structured methodology and problem formulation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing GRPO algorithm with a straightforward reward function (r_per + r_eff) to existing ZipVL mechanism, without meaningful algorithmic innovation

Critical missing evaluation: no wall-clock inference time, memory usage, or end-to-end latency measurements despite claiming efficiency gains; token reduction does not guarantee practical speedup due to sparse operation overhead
Insufficient ablation studies: no analysis of KL weight β, reward weighting justification, number of samples N, reference model choice, or sensitivity to key hyperparameters
Training-inference distribution mismatch: model trained with p~U(0,1) but deployed with fixed p=0.975; this mismatch and its impact are not addressed
No comparison with related sparse attention methods (MOBA, NSA, structured regularization) mentioned in introduction, limiting understanding of relative contributions

Technical clarity issues: unclear how gradients flow through non-differentiable Top-p selection mechanism (Eq. 3), computational cost of post-training not discussed, 'sampling group' concept inadequately explained
Limited scope: evaluation restricted to Qwen2/2.5-VL family only; generalization to other MLLM architectures unknown

Shallow analysis of performance degradation: while claimed 'minimal', shows non-negligible drops on specific benchmarks (e.g., TextVQA 82.0→81.3); no analysis of failure modes or affected question types
Reproducibility concerns: sparse details on Video-R1-260k dataset, incomplete hyperparameter specifications, differences in evaluation settings noted relative to official reports

Reward function design unjustified: equal weighting of performance/efficiency not motivated, binary performance reward is coarse-grained, no exploration of Pareto-optimal efficiency-performance tradeoffs

strengths: Clear problem motivation: identifies and addresses a genuine limitation of existing sparse attention methods that plateau at ~50% token reduction
Novel reward formulation using grouped-rollout GRPO with conditional efficiency reward that elegantly handles cases where no rollout achieves correctness

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 13 diverse benchmarks (7 image, 6 video) with multiple model families and strong baselines including ZipVL, VisionZip, FastV, Minference, MOBA, and sharpness loss
Impressive empirical results: achieves 20-25% token retention compared to ZipVL's 75-80% with maintained or improved accuracy, and demonstrates 3.3× latency speedup and 3× memory reduction
Thorough ablation studies examining sparse attention mechanisms (top-k, top-p, threshold), budget sampling ranges, and group sizes
Practical deployment focus: explicitly addresses inference-aligned token pruning and KV-cache management
Robustness analysis on HallusionBench and investigation of scalability across model sizes and sequence lengths
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components are from existing work (top-p sparse attention from ZipVL, GRPO from Shao et al. 2024); contribution is primarily engineering-focused with a simple reward function design

Training efficiency inadequately addressed: paper acknowledges sequential rollout execution 'precludes straightforward batching and slows training' but provides no wall-clock time comparison with baselines, which is critical for practical adoption

Severe generalization limitations: experiments restricted to Qwen2/Qwen2.5-VL and LLaVA-Video; no evaluation on other major MLLM architectures (LLaMA-Vision, Phi-Vision, etc.), making broad applicability unclear

Incomplete baseline analysis: MOBA and sharpness loss drop dramatically to 66.2-66.8 vs. full model's 70.0; insufficient analysis of whether this gap reflects unfair comparison or implementation issues

Reward function design lacks justification: group-level indicator C (Eq. 8) creating binary efficiency conditions appears ad-hoc with no ablation study; method doesn't differentiate multiple correct rollouts by efficiency

Misleading inference-time deployment claim: during inference p is fixed to 0.975 despite training with varied p∈[0.94, 0.975], discarding learned budget-accuracy tradeoff information and contradicting 'controllable trade-offs' claim
Insufficient analysis of design choices: reference model selection and KL weight β=0.04 lack ablation studies; no exploration of alternative reward formulations or lower p ranges
Limited statistical rigor: no error bars or significance testing; HallusionBench results show 'minor fluctuations' without quantitative analysis
Missing error analysis and interpretability: no investigation of which token types/positions are pruned, per-task performance degradation, or learned sparsity patterns across layers
Reproducibility concerns: no reported code availability, actual training time/computational costs omitted, KV-cache implementation details missing
